n1.text: System pressure is low. Let's start at the source. Check the main air supply valve to this machine — is it open? And what does the supply gauge read?
n1.hint: The main shutoff valve is usually a quarter-turn ball valve on the drop from the overhead air main. Should be parallel to the pipe = open.

options.label: Valve is closed or supply is low
options.transition: Found it — no supply, no pressure. Simple as that.

options.label: Valve is open, supply reads normal
options.transition: Supply is fine. The problem is between the supply and the machine. Let's narrow it down.

n2.text: Listen carefully around the machine. Can you hear any air leaking? A hissing sound, even a faint one, means you're losing pressure somewhere.
n2.hint: Check fittings, hoses, cylinders, and valve manifolds. Soapy water on connections will bubble at a leak.

options.label: Yes, I can hear a leak
options.transition: Air leak found. Every leak is like leaving a faucet running — it drains your supply.

options.label: No obvious leaks
options.transition: No leaks. Let's check the filter and regulator.

n3.text: Check the FRL unit (Filter-Regulator-Lubricator). Is the filter bowl full of water or contamination? And what's the regulator set to?
n3.hint: The filter bowl should be mostly clear. A water-logged filter restricts airflow. The regulator gauge should show your required operating pressure (typically 80-90 PSI).

options.label: Filter is clogged/full
options.transition: Clogged filter is choking the air supply. That's an easy fix.

options.label: Regulator is set too low
options.transition: The regulator is limiting the pressure. Just needs adjustment.

options.label: Both look OK
options.transition: FRL is fine. The issue might be the compressor or the main air system.

n_supply.text: The main air supply to the machine is shut off or the plant air system pressure is low. This is upstream of the machine.
steps: Open the supply valve if it was closed (someone may have shut it during maintenance)
If plant air is low, check the compressor — is it running?
Check for a large leak somewhere else in the plant that's dragging down system pressure
Verify the machine's supply pressure comes up to operating range before restarting

n_leak.text: Air leak is draining your pressure. Fix the leak and pressure should recover.
steps: Locate the exact leak point — spray soapy water on suspect fittings and watch for bubbles
Tighten loose fittings (hand-tight plus one turn with a wrench)
Replace cracked or cut hoses
Check cylinder rod seals — worn seals leak at the rod
After repairs, monitor pressure to verify it holds

n_filter.text: The air filter is clogged with water or contamination, restricting airflow to the machine.
steps: Drain the filter bowl — open the drain petcock at the bottom
If the filter element is discolored or damaged, replace it
Check the auto-drain if one is installed — it may be stuck closed
If you're getting a lot of water, the plant air dryer may need service
Set a PM reminder to check the filter weekly

n_regulator.text: The regulator is set below the required operating pressure. Simple adjustment.
steps: Pull up on the regulator knob to unlock it
Turn clockwise to increase pressure to the required setpoint
Push the knob back down to lock it
Verify downstream pressure stabilizes at the new setpoint
If the regulator won't hold pressure, it may need replacement

n_compressor.text: Machine-side components are fine. The issue is likely the plant air compressor or main distribution system.
steps: Check compressor status — is it running? Any faults displayed?
Check the receiver tank pressure — if it's low, the compressor can't keep up with demand
Look for large leaks in the main air distribution system
If the compressor is running but can't build pressure, it may need service (valves, rings, or motor)
Contact facilities/maintenance for plant air system issues
